$comment: T-3578 format, the smooth style (T-3696; docs/AUDIO.md § Narration style): the same words as the panel shows, with ElevenLabs v3 audio tags in square brackets and [short pause]/[long pause] and ellipses for pauses, a pause at each change of subject, no whispering, at most one laugh. Performance only: a tone is a reading, not evidence of how anyone spoke (L-jaunt-voices-3578). Keyed <part>:<id>.

scripts.opening:opening:
[measured] Fort Dearborn, Building by Building.

[short pause] Friday, 14 August 1812, the last full day of the first Fort Dearborn. [short pause] The United States built this post in 1803, when Captain John Whistler's company marched in from Detroit and put it up in logs on the south bank of the Chicago River. In 1808 Whistler drew every building for the War Department. [short pause] Since 1810 the commander has been Captain Nathan Heald, with 'fifty-four regulars and twelve militia'. On 18 June the United States declared war on Britain; the news reached here in July. [short pause] Five days ago an order came from the general at Detroit: abandon the post. Tomorrow at nine the garrison marches out of the gate. [short pause] Today everyone is packing, giving away and destroying what cannot be carried, and waiting.

[short pause] Twelve stops, daybreak to sunset, with the clock moving through the day. By tomorrow night every building you are about to see but one will be ash. [short pause] Watch for the one that survives.
scripts.stop:the-fort: [measured] 14 August 1812, daybreak. [short pause] This is the first Fort Dearborn, seen from outside. [short pause] Captain John Whistler's company reached this bend of the river in 1803, 'at two o'clock on the afternoon of August 17', where the bank stood 'eight feet high', and built the whole post in logs with their own hands. [short pause] A visitor from Fort Wayne in 1809 called it 'the neatest and best wooden garrison in the United States'. Barracks round a square, two gun blockhouses at opposite corners, and a double ring of pickets. [short pause] Nine years on, the order has come to abandon it, and tomorrow morning everyone inside will leave. Today is their last full day here. [short pause] It starts, like every day in this fort, at the gate.
scripts.stop:the-gate: [measured] Six in the morning, at the main gate, in the middle of the south side. [short pause] A girl who lived here remembered that sunset was 'when they used to shut the gates of the fort'. Notice the two rows of pickets. [short pause] An attacker who got over the first 'would only find himself within a narrow inclosure', swept by fire from the blockhouses at the corners. Whistler built this fort to stand a siege. [short pause] No one is planning to stand one now: the order is to march out, and this is the gate they will use. [short pause] Walk on through the gate and step inside to where the soldiers live.
scripts.stop:soldiers: [measured] Seven in the morning, just inside the gate. [short pause] The soldiers' barracks flank it on both sides, two storeys with 'shingled Roofs and Galliaries fronting the parade'. The first company here built the fort themselves, and when their enlistments ran out 'they had all re-enlisted'. [short pause] Whistler's letters show how far this post was from anything: he had 'sixty-six men to supply' with fifty-six suits of clothes, and 'two fifers but the only fife has been lost.' [short pause] The garrison now is 'fifty-four regulars and twelve militia', and this morning they are packing for the long march to Fort Wayne. The man who will lead them lives across the parade. [short pause] Five days ago he made a choice his own officers begged him not to make.
scripts.stop:commandant: [measured] Half past eight, on the parade. [short pause] In the middle stands the 'lofty flagstaff'; on the east side, the commanding officer's quarters. Captain Nathan Heald has commanded here since 1810. In June 1811 he brought his bride Rebekah, 'the niece of Captain William Wells' of Fort Wayne. [short pause] Wau-Bun has her and Mrs. Helm 'playing at battledoor' in the quarters last spring. In May, Heald wrote, 'we had a son born dead for the want of a skilful Midwife.' [short pause] General Hull's order to abandon the post arrived on 9 August and 'was read next morning upon parade', here. The officers' 'unanimous advice was, to remain where they were, and fortify themselves as strongly as possible.' Heald chose to obey. [short pause] Those officers live directly opposite, and tomorrow they will march out behind him.
scripts.stop:officers: [measured] Ten o'clock, the officers' barracks, facing the commandant. [short pause] Three men live here. Lieutenant Linai Helm, Heald's second in command, asked to come from Detroit for 'the cheaper cost of living'; his wife Margaret is the 'step-daughter of old John Kinzie', the trader across the river. [short pause] Ensign George Ronan, the junior officer, is 'a young cadet direct from West Point'. And the surgeon's mate, Dr. Isaac Van Voorhis, twenty-two, who wrote last October that this place would one day be 'the seat of millions yet unborn'. [short pause] By tomorrow noon Ronan and Van Voorhis will be dead and Helm a prisoner. [short pause] On the north side of the parade stands the one building in this fort that will still be standing next spring.
scripts.stop:magazine: [measured] Eleven o'clock, the north side. [short pause] Ahead is the magazine, where powder is kept: 'a small structure made of brick', in a fort built of logs. Beside it, the north-west blockhouse and its cannon, and 'A small wicket gate' through the pickets. [short pause] To the right, the north range, part barracks and part 'the contractor's store of supplies'. When the fort burns, this little building 'alone defied the fire'. [short pause] Seven months from now a British agent, Robert Dickson, will find that 'The powder magazine was in a good state of preservation'. But the fort's spare ammunition is no longer anywhere in these buildings. [short pause] Last night it was carried out in secret, to the north-east corner, and down a well.
scripts.stop:covered-way: [measured] Noon, the north-east corner. [short pause] From here a covered way ran down to the river, so the garrison could reach water 'in time of attack'. Whistler listed it on his drawing but left it off: 'Omited in their places'. [short pause] Wau-Bun calls it a sally-port, with a well dug inside. Last night the ammunition and liquor 'were carried, part into the sally-port, and thrown into a well'. [short pause] The muskets 'were broken up and thrown into the well' after them, and the whiskey barrels were knocked in and poured into the river. Heald feared they 'would make bad use of it'. [short pause] It was no secret: by this morning 'the taste of the water' was 'strong grog'. Everyone outside the pickets now knows the guns are gone. [short pause] Outside the south-east corner, the traders are counting what is left.
scripts.stop:merchants: [measured] Half past one, outside the pickets on the south-east. [short pause] Here stood the merchant's shop, the sutler's garden, and the armourer's shop, where the garrison's guns were kept in repair. The sutler is the private trader licensed to sell to the soldiers; since January that has been 'Messrs. [short pause] Kinzie & Forsyth', John Kinzie's firm. Behind you rises the south-east blockhouse, the fort's second gun corner. Whistler's drawing puts the blockhouses north-west and south-east; Wau-Bun, written forty years later, remembered both 'on the southern side'. [short pause] South of here, the gardens are full of a summer's growing that the garrison will not stay to eat.
scripts.stop:gardens: [measured] Three in the afternoon, the commanding officer's gardens, south of the fort, where in the early years 'melons and other small fruit and vegetables were raised'. [short pause] Whistler had the brush cleared 'all within one Fourth of a Mile of the Garrison', so nobody could creep up unseen. Beyond lies what he called 'a large parraria', open grass, and the line of woods along the South Branch. [short pause] Tomorrow the column will go the other way: east to the lake, then south along the beach, 'with the lake on our left, and a high sand bank on our right'. [short pause] West of here, at the government's trading house, the last of the goods are being handed out.
scripts.stop:agency: [measured] Half past four, west of the fort, among the government houses: the factor's trading house, the agent's house, the interpreter's, the bake house and the stables. [short pause] The factor runs the government's own store. Heald's report for today: 'On the 14th, I delivered the Indians all the goods in the factory store, and a considerable quantity of provisions which we could not take away with us.' [short pause] Out went 'blankets, broadcloths, calicoes, paints'. [short pause] In April the townspeople had fortified the agency house, 'an old-fashioned log building, with a hall running through the centre', and its piazzas 'were planked up, for greater security, port-holes were cut, and sentinels posted at night.' [short pause] Now the shelves are bare. [short pause] The day's last light is falling on the river, below the fort.
scripts.stop:wharf: [measured] Six in the evening, at the wharf, below the bank on the river side, where boats tied up and the fort's stores came ashore. [short pause] In 1808 Whistler judged the garrison 'perfectly secure from any ambuscade', except for one thing: the houses across the river, 'somewhat in the way'. [short pause] He had already pulled up a picket fence over there that 'might serve as a Barrier against the Garrison'. The biggest of those houses, straight across the water, belongs to John Kinzie. [short pause] His family will not march with the soldiers tomorrow; they are going by boat. [short pause] Walk along the bank and face it as the sun goes down on the fort's last night.
scripts.stop:across-the-river: [measured] Sunset. [short pause] Across the river, 'John Kinzie Esq. House on the opisite side River', and three more houses to the west. Kinzie sells to the garrison and lives within shouting distance of the gate. [short pause] Behind you, the gates are shutting at sunset, for the last time. Tomorrow 'at 9 o'clock in the morning' they will open, the band will strike up 'the Dead March', and the garrison will walk out. [short pause] The morning after, the fort is set on fire, and only the brick magazine comes through. [short pause] The army will come back in 1816 and build a second fort on this ground.
scripts.ending:burned: [solemnly] On 15 August 1812 the garrison marched out of the gate. Heald wrote afterwards that the warriors 'set fire to the fort and left the place, taking the prisoners with them.' [short pause] Seven months later Robert Dickson found the brick magazine standing and 'The powder magazine was in a good state of preservation'. Everything else Whistler built was ash. [short pause] For four years 'over Chicago silence and desolation reigned supreme', until the army came back in 1816 and built again on the same ground. [short pause] To follow the garrison out of the gate on the morning of the 15th, take the jaunt The Battle of Fort Dearborn.
